course/17-concurrency/01-threads-lesson..first:
# 01. Threads

**Tier:** Deep. **Why you'd use this:** Several slow network waits should overlap instead of running one after another. Threads help with waiting; the GIL still serializes pure Python bytecode.

**After this lesson you can:** overlap waits with threads; run work in a `ThreadPoolExecutor`; explain what the GIL serializes.
About 30 minutes. **Uses:** [Context managers](../12-data-model/02-context-managers-lesson.ipynb)
course/17-concurrency/01-threads-lesson..quick_review:
## Quick review

1. What does `with` guarantee about a context manager?
2. Name one reason to prefer a pool over starting raw `Thread` objects by hand.

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

`__exit__` runs on the way out, even after an error. A pool caps workers and gives you futures for results.
</details>

course/17-concurrency/02-processes-lesso.first:
# 02. Processes

**Tier:** Deep. **Why you'd use this:** Heavy CPU work does not overlap well under the GIL. Separate processes can use more than one core, if the function and its data can be pickled.

**After this lesson you can:** choose a process pool when CPU work should use more cores; map a picklable function across workers; explain why lambdas fail under spawn.
About 25 minutes. **Uses:** [Threads](01-threads-lesson.ipynb)
course/17-concurrency/02-processes-lesso.quick_review:
## Quick review

1. What kind of work do threads help most with?
2. What does the GIL serialize?

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

Waiting (I/O). Pure Python bytecode on one object graph in a process.
</details>

course/17-concurrency/03-async-lesson.ip.first:
# 03. Async

**Tier:** Deep. **Why you'd use this:** Many small waits can share one thread if each task yields at `await`. You gather results in order without a thread per wait.

**After this lesson you can:** overlap `await` sleeps; gather results in order; start a loop from a script without calling `asyncio.run` inside a notebook.
About 30 minutes. **Uses:** [Threads](01-threads-lesson.ipynb)
course/17-concurrency/03-async-lesson.ip.quick_review:
## Quick review

1. When do processes beat threads for speed?
2. Why must a `ProcessPoolExecutor` target be picklable?

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

CPU-bound work that needs more than one core. Workers are separate interpreters that receive the function by pickling.
</details>

course/17-concurrency/04-race-conditions.first:
# 04. Race conditions

**Tier:** Deep. **Why you'd use this:** Two threads update the same counter with `+=` and you lose increments. A lock makes the read–modify–write step exclusive.

**After this lesson you can:** explain a lost update from unlocked `+=`; make the race visible with read–sleep–write; protect the counter with a `Lock`.
About 30 minutes. **Uses:** [Threads](01-threads-lesson.ipynb)
course/17-concurrency/04-race-conditions.quick_review:
## Quick review

1. What does `await` do to the current task?
2. Why avoid `asyncio.run` inside a notebook cell that already has a loop?

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

It pauses that task so others can run until the wait finishes. The notebook already has a running loop — nest or use top-level await instead.
</details>

course/17-concurrency/05-taskgroup-timeo.first:
# 05. TaskGroup and timeouts

**Tier:** Deep. **Why you'd use this:** Several async jobs should start together, fail together, and respect a deadline. `TaskGroup` and `asyncio.timeout` give you that structure.

**After this lesson you can:** run coroutines in a `TaskGroup`; cancel work with `asyncio.timeout`; explain that a failure cancels siblings.
About 30 minutes. **Uses:** [Async](03-async-lesson.ipynb)
course/17-concurrency/05-taskgroup-timeo.quick_review:
## Quick review

1. Why can unlocked `+=` lose updates across threads?
2. What does a `Lock` protect?

<details><summary>Answers</summary>

Read–modify–write is not one atomic step. The critical section you wrap so only one thread runs it at a time.
</details>
